title: DACA Recipient Sues Government After Deportation Triggers 'Unauthorized Travel' Termination Notice
excerpt: Jessica Treviño, whose DACA status was valid through April 2027, was deported in March and now faces termination of her protections for leaving the country.
body:
• Jessica Treviño, 34, has filed a federal lawsuit challenging her deportation to Mexico despite holding valid DACA status through April 2027.
  • USCIS sent Treviño a notice terminating her DACA for 'unauthorized travel' — citing the date of her own deportation as the unauthorized departure.
  • As of February 2026, over 261 DACA recipients had been detained and more than 86 deported, many with valid, unexpired status.
  • Advocates call the case a deliberate Catch-22 designed to systematically dismantle DACA protections without formal policy change.

A Texas mother who was deported to Mexico despite holding valid DACA status has filed a federal lawsuit against the U.S. government after receiving a notice that her protections would be terminated for "unauthorized travel" — travel that consisted of her own forced deportation.

Jessica Treviño, 34, arrived in the United States at age 7 and received DACA protections at 20. Her status was valid through April 2027 when federal agents detained her and her husband in a Home Depot parking lot in South Texas in December 2025. She was deported to Matamoros, Mexico, on March 25, 2026.

The Catch-22

Weeks after her removal, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services sent Treviño a notice of intent to terminate her DACA status, citing "unauthorized travel outside of the United States on or about March 25, 2026" — the exact date the Department of Homeland Security deported her.

Under DACA rules, recipients must remain in the United States and are prohibited from traveling abroad without advance parole. The government's argument effectively creates what immigration advocates call a Catch-22: deport a recipient, then cite the deportation as grounds to strip their status.

"This is a deliberate, systematic effort to destroy DACA. The government is removing people first and then using that removal as the basis to terminate their protections."

— Todd Schulte, President of FWD.us

Three Children Left Behind

Treviño's three children — ages 16, 14, and 13 — are all U.S. citizens and are living with a family member near the Texas border while their parents remain in Matamoros. The family separation began when federal agents followed Treviño and her husband into a parking lot before arresting them both.

Attorney David Rozas filed the lawsuit seeking three forms of relief: a declaration that Treviño's deportation was unlawful, government assistance with her return to the United States, and restoration of her DACA status to its previous standing.

A Pattern of Enforcement

Treviño's case is not isolated. As of February 2026, more than 261 DACA recipients had been detained and over 86 deported, many while holding valid, unexpired protections. The government has not released updated data for the remainder of 2026.

The enforcement pattern coincides with multiple legal and administrative challenges to the program. In April 2026, the Board of Immigration Appeals issued a precedential decision finding that holding DACA alone is insufficient reason to terminate removal proceedings — a ruling that further weakened the program's protective framework.

Separately, a Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals decision found DACA's grant of work authorization unlawful while suggesting its deportation protections could be treated separately. A federal judge in Texas is considering how to implement that ruling, with a proposal that could revoke work permits for DACA recipients who move into Texas.

What's at Stake

Nearly 530,000 people currently hold DACA protections. Advocates say the Treviño case represents a template for dismantling the program case by case, without the political costs of a formal policy change or public announcement.

The Department of Homeland Security had not issued a formal comment on the lawsuit as of late July. USCIS's termination notice remained active.

For the Indian community, the case resonates with broader concerns about immigration enforcement and the security of deferred action programs. Indian DACA recipients, while fewer in number than their Latino counterparts, face the same procedural vulnerabilities that the Treviño case exposes.

nri_angle: The case highlights vulnerabilities in deferred action programs that also affect Indian DACA recipients and raises concerns about the broader immigration enforcement climate.
